cases.abstract: Vector-Quantized Behavior Transformers (VQ-BeT) model multimodal robot behavior by learning action tokens from uncurated behavior data rather than assigning actions to k-means bins. Residual vector quantization encodes each action or action chunk with a coarse code followed by a code for the unrepresented embedding residual. A transformer predicts these codes from observation histories with optional goal conditioning; their vectors are summed, decoded, and refined by a continuous offset. Actions are thus generated in one forward pass rather than by iterative denoising. In simulated manipulation and locomotion, VQ-BeT generally matches or exceeds the tested baselines in task performance, while entropy measurements and rollouts show diverse behaviors; diffusion policies nevertheless lead on unconditional Image Kitchen and BlockPush. On a low-cost mobile manipulator, controller noise disrupts receding-horizon rollouts, so all policies are evaluated fully closed-loop. Single-phase totals are similar (47/50 versus 45/50), but VQ-BeT completes 19/30 two-phase trials versus 11/30 for an adapted DiffusionPolicy-T. Onboard CPU inference takes 207.25 ms versus 5243.82 ms, reducing the computational cost of generating a fresh action at every step.
cases.results: The hardware comparison shows a larger aggregate success advantage for VQ-BeT on sequences than on standalone tasks. With fully closed-loop execution and ten trials per task, VQ-BeT and the adapted DiffusionPolicy-T complete 47/50 and 45/50 single-phase trials, respectively, compared with 19/30 and 11/30 two-phase trials. The aggregate gain does not extend to every sequence: on closing both doors, diffusion succeeds in 6/10 trials versus 5/10 for VQ-BeT, which nonetheless generates both possible closing orders. Final completion rates on each of four longer sequences are at least three times the baseline's. The timing comparison matters for this platform because controller noise disrupted receding-horizon rollouts, prompting action prediction at every step. On the robot's onboard CPU, average inference takes 207.25 ms for VQ-BeT versus 5243.82 ms for diffusion. Thus, higher aggregate sequence completion accompanies faster per-step prediction under the evaluated closed-loop protocol.

cases.abstract: In sparse-reward robot learning, imitation can supply candidate actions while an online actor is still ineffective. Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) keeps imitation and RL policies separate: a target critic selects between their proposals for both interaction and temporal-difference bootstrapping, greedily or by value-weighted sampling. The bootstrap target therefore evaluates the same hybrid selection rule used to collect experience, instead of relying on the RL actor alone. Policy separation also accommodates different architecture preferences observed in Robomimic: ResNet-18 performs better for cloning, whereas the proposed shallow vision-transformer architecture performs better in online RL. Actor dropout improves sample efficiency and also benefits regularized fine-tuning; retaining it does not prevent performance losses when either proposal mechanism is removed. IBRL outperforms demonstration oversampling and regularized fine-tuning on Robomimic, while performing similarly to fine-tuning on simpler Meta-World tasks. In real-robot cloth hanging with manual resets, 30 demonstrations and 30,000 interaction steps yield 85% success for IBRL versus 65% for cloning, 35% for fine-tuning, and 15% for oversampling, in 20 evaluation trials per method.
cases.results: On the deformable-cloth Hang task, IBRL improves on the reference imitation policy, whereas both alternative demonstration-assisted RL methods finish below it. Each RL method uses 30 demonstrations and 30,000 interaction steps; final-checkpoint success is 85% for IBRL, 35% for regularized fine-tuning, and 15% for RLPD, versus 65% for the demonstration-trained cloning policy. These final-checkpoint evaluations use 20 trials per method with shared initial conditions, yielding a 20-percentage-point improvement over cloning. The hardware protocol uses sparse success rewards and manual resets. Complementary Robomimic Square ablations show that actor dropout improves the baselines without closing the gap to IBRL; removing either imitation-based action proposal or bootstrap proposal degrades IBRL even with dropout retained. The ablations support both proposal mechanisms beyond actor regularization, while Hang documents improvement over the reference policy within the hardware budget.
